title: BLAD: Test Dataset for Bilingual Acronym Disambiguation for Dutch and English Domain-Specific Text
abstract: We have curated a dataset of multi-sense acronym usage within the documentation of an established power company, given a list of acronyms known to be actively in use. Dataset contains 176 unique sentences for 126 multi-sense acronyms. Some acronym senses could not be found in the documents, for these we do not have an example sentence. The senses vary between two and five per acronym. As such, the internal disambiguation is a multi-class problem with a median of two classes (expansions) per acronym. Of the examples, 26 are in English, while the rest are in Dutch. Every expansion is annotated with a language tag (en/nl). Each expansion term is also annotated according to its domain specificity as "global" (has a dedicated Wikipedia page), "domain-specific" (acronym and expansion occur together at least more than once in Web search results) and "company" (used only within the company) \textit{(see Table 1 for distribution)}. The "domain-specific" category does not refer to a specific domain here - the examples vary across domains such as energy/electricity and information technology/business intelligence.

title: AI in the Next Five Years: Navigating Strategic Uncertainty
abstract: AI fundamentally transforms decision-making, organizational structures, competitive dynamics, and leadership imperatives. AI has become an essential force reshaping business and society, bringing unprecedented opportunities and significant risks. Strategic clarity in the age of AI will not emerge from eliminating uncertainty but rather from becoming adept at navigating it. The C-suite must embrace strategic agility, preparedness, and continual learning as corner stones of leadership that will win the future. The generative AI boom triggered by ChatGPT's launch in late 2022 has produced genuine capability and inflated expectations in equal measure. For executives seeking competitive advantage, neither the technoutopian nor the defensive doomer position serves. Most AI forecasts focus on what will be destroyed: jobs eliminated, industries disrupted, companies made obsolete.

title: Thinking with Images without Coordinates
abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal large language models have shifted toward the "thinking with images" paradigm to improve reasoning faithfulness, yet existing methods rely heavily on explicit coordinate- based grounding. We identify two fundamental limitations in this approach, i.e., a semantic gap where sparse regressions miss high-dimensional latent structures, and a resolution gap due to the granularity mismatch between patch-level tokens and pixel-level coordinates. To address these, we propose TiCO (Thinking with images without COordinates). It reformulates visual reasoning as a semantic evidence discovery process within the latent space, and evidence is injected as token-level regions without pixel coordinates. Specifically, TiCO utilizes a dedicated probe token to estimate similarity distributions and performs importance sampling over spatially connected components to generate diverse, semantically dominant evidence rollouts. Extensive experiments across multiple high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our TiCO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art coordinate-based methods with significantly improved inference efficiency.

title: Knowing Whether, Not Just Where: Anchor-Probing Distillation for Open-Set Remote Sensing Visual Grounding
abstract: Open-set visual grounding in remote sensing requires models to determine not only where a queried object is located, but also whether the image provides sufficient evidence for the query at all. Existing closed-set grounding models, however, tend to return plausible boxes even for absent objects, blurring localization confidence with genuine Visual Support. We introduce AnchorProbe-Distill (APD), a teacher-student framework that recasts open-set grounding as Visual Support learning. APD builds on the insight that supported queries should induce coherent spatial anchors, whereas unsupported or mismatched queries tend to produce unstable or misleading localization patterns. APD-T therefore uses the Original Query as a Reference Anchor to interpret query perturbations: Semantic-Preserving Queries retain the annotated target, Near-Category Ambiguous Queries are resolved according to whether they form a reliable alternative anchor or collapse onto the Reference Anchor, and Far-Category Counterfactual Queries provide rejection supervision. This reference-aware reasoning is distilled into APD-S, enabling unified localization and rejection from a single image--query pair. Experiments show that APD enables the resulting model to reject absent targets while also improving its localization of present targets.

title: Modelling Josephson Junctions with Boundary Conditions: Towards High-Fidelity Models for Superconducting Qubits
abstract: Josephson junctions are the central nonlinear element of superconducting qubits, yet their standard description is reached through a chain of approximations. We propose a purely quantum-mechanical model of the junction, formulated directly in Hilbert space: a charged particle moves on a one-dimensional loop, and the junction is a point at which the wave function obeys self-adjoint boundary conditions, labelled by a coupling strength $λ$, which controls the transparency of the junction, and a phase jump $δ$, which plays the role of the superconducting phase difference. For a loop with a single junction we solve the spectral problem and show that the ground-state momentum expectation, identified with the supercurrent, factorises exactly as $\langle\hat{p}_0\rangle = I_c(δ,λ)\sinδ$. For opaque junctions $I_c$ becomes independent of $δ$ and the first Josephson relation $I=I_c\sinδ$ is recovered; for strongly attractive coupling, where the ground state is bound to the junction, the $\sinδ$ law is also recovered, but with an exponentially suppressed amplitude. For more transparent junctions, however, the model \emph{predicts} deviations from the pure $\sinδ$ law: $I_c$ acquires a dependence on $δ$ already at order $λ^{-2}$, compatible with the higher Josephson harmonics recently found necessary to describe superconducting qubit spectra, and a fully transparent contact yields a current linear in $δ$. When the phase varies in time, a gauge transformation shows that the voltage drop across the junction is proportional to $\dotδ$, so that the second Josephson relation emerges without being imposed. The boundary-condition approach thus reproduces both Josephson relations from first principles and predicts corrections to them, offering a route towards higher-fidelity models of superconducting qubits.

title: Scalable Quantum Clustering of Renewable Profiles via a Hybrid Qubit-efficient Strategy
abstract: Large-scale renewable energy profile clustering is a computationally challenging NP-hard problem. Recent quantum computing techniques offer a potential remedy, yet their scalability is severely constrained by the limited qubit count of current quantum hardware. To address this issue, we first cast the problem into a QUBO form and then we propose a consensus-based variable reduction (CBVR) method to drastically cut qubit usage. More specifically, we tailor the one-hot constraint to eliminate assignment variables and leverage consensus analysis to convert stable clustering relations from initial anneals into equality constraints for further reduction. Experiments on real quantum hardware confirm that CBVR compresses oversized QUBO models into feasible sizes while retaining high clustering quality and efficiency.

title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.

evidence.title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
evidence.abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.

title: RAMP: Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision for Efficient Prefill in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
abstract: Recurrent-depth language models improve inference-time reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared network to refine internal representations, but the additional recurrent computation also increases inference cost. This overhead is particularly pronounced during long-context prefill, where the full input sequence is repeatedly processed across recurrent depth. Weight-and-activation quantization offers a natural way to accelerate this computation through lower-precision arithmetic, yet repeatedly applying quantized computation introduces numerical perturbations that accumulate along the recurrent trajectory. We systematically analyze how such errors propagate across recurrent depth and show that quantization errors introduced earlier are attenuated by more subsequent recurrent steps and therefore have a smaller effect on the final representation. Matched-budget experiments strongly support this prediction, showing that placing quantized computation earlier in recurrent depth consistently yields the best fidelity. Based on this insight, we introduce RAMP (Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision), which performs early recurrent refinement using low-precision weight-and-activation computation and restores high precision for terminal refinement. Across context lengths up to 4K, RAMP preserves near-full-precision prefill quality while achieving up to 1.16x end-to-end first-prefill speedup on an NVIDIA H100, corresponding to a 13.9% latency reduction.

title: Inverse Synthesis of Shock Time Series from Shock Response Spectra Using Ensembles of Conditional Variational Autoencoders
abstract: The shock response spectrum (SRS) characterizes the peak responses of single-degree-of-freedom systems to transient acceleration. Because the mapping from an acceleration time series (waveform) to its SRS is many-to-one, inverse synthesis seeks candidate waveforms consistent with a prescribed spectrum. We extend an earlier conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) framework with a recurrent decoder that predicts multiscale wavelet coefficients and reconstructs waveforms through an inverse discrete wavelet transform. Individual models exhibit limited variability under latent sampling, motivating an ensemble of independently trained models spanning different mother wavelets and decomposition levels. Each member produces a separate candidate waveform for the same target SRS. Evaluation on four held-out benchmark datasets shows lower mean and median spectral errors for the illustrated wavelet model than for the earlier direct time-domain CVAE and a sum-of-decayed-sinusoids (SDS) baseline. A conditioning study examines frequency-grid and encoding choices. Comparisons with published inverse-SRS methods demonstrate superior performance across four holdout benchmark datasets (two operational shock datasets, one earthquake dataset, and one synthetic shock dataset) and competitive performance on synthetic targets reported by Brake. Single-model inference requires approximately 0.1-0.6 ms per waveform during batched inference compared with 5-8 s for SDS, excluding offline training. This low inference cost enables rapid generation of distinct SRS-compatible candidate waveforms across the ensemble, although their physical suitability requires assessment beyond spectral agreement.

title: Continuous-time evolution via probabilistic angle interpolation and its applications
abstract: We explore the applicability of a stochastic time-evolution algorithm based on probabilistic angle interpolation. To simplify the pre-processing of the algorithm, we take the continuous-time limit, thereby explicitly eliminating Trotter errors and streamlining the resource analysis. We also introduce a noise-mitigation method tailored to it. As demonstrations, we apply the algorithm to two representative problems: estimating the ground-state energy of the $H_3^+$ molecular Hamiltonian and computing out-of-time-ordered correlators in the sparse Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev model. We evaluate the protocol's performance through numerical simulations and experiments on a trapped-ion quantum computer, Quantinuum Reimei.

title: Mapping the Intersection of Neuromarketing and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into neuromarketing has significantly transformed how consumer behavior is analyzed, interpreted, and influenced. By combining neuroscientific methods with advanced computational techniques, neuromarketing allows for the exploration of subconscious cognitive and emotional processes that traditional market research methods often fail to capture. Despite this growing body of research, the literature remains fragmented and conceptually dispersed, limiting a structured understanding of its intellectual foundations, thematic evolution, and future research directions. The results reveal a strong growth trajectory in neuromarketing research with AI, reflecting the increasing academic and managerial interest in data-driven and neuro-informed decision-making. It provides a conceptual basis for future research and assists researchers and practitioners in understanding the opportunities and challenges associated with the responsible and effective use of artificial intelligence in neuromarketing contexts

title: Artificial Intelligence in Marketing From Predictive Analytics to Generative Creativity
abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the foundations of modern marketing, shifting from data-driven decision-making toward an era of intelligent creativity that fuses predictive analytics with generative innovation. This chapter conceptually examines how the integration of predictive and generative AI—through the Integrated Predictive–Generative Framework (IPGF)—redefines marketing intelligence by merging analytical precision with creative synthesis. Through theoretical analysis and case-based interpretation, the chapter explores predictive AI in forecasting consumer behavior and generative AI in producing personalized, emotionally resonant content. It also identifies ethical, psychological, and social implications associated with AI-driven creativity, emphasizing transparency, fairness, and human oversight as essential principles for sustainable, human-centered marketing ecosystems.

title: Impacto de datos sintéticos generados mediante CTGAN en modelos de aprendizaje automático para la predicción
abstract: The objective of this study was to evaluate comparatively the predictive performance and explainability of Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost trained on real data versus real data augmented with CTGAN. This research is computational/experimental in nature, focusing on predictive models, with a quantitative approach, a comparative purpose, and an applied orientation. The results revealed findings contrary to what is reported in most of the literature reviewed: adding synthetic data to the training did not improve the predictive performance of any of the three models but rather reduced it in a statistically significant manner, even when that same synthetic data passed statistical fidelity validation compared to the real data. In conclusion, at the theoretical level, the study provides a concrete example of the relationship between statistical fidelity and the predictive utility of synthetic data an aspect that remains largely unexplored in the reviewed literature.

title: MaLeFiz - Maschinelles Lernen zur effizienten Identifikation auffälliger Finanztransaktionen; Teilvorhaben "Technikentwicklung"
abstract: Im Rahmen des Projekts MaLeFiz wurden im Teilvorhaben "Technikentwicklung" Methoden des maschinellen Lernens zur Identifikation auffälliger Finanztransaktionen (Geldwäscheerkennung) entwickelt und evaluiert. Nach anfänglicher Literaturrecherche und Grundlagenschaffung musste aufgrund des Ausbleibens einer Datenspende durch eine Bank auf synthetische Daten zurückgegriffen werden. Hierzu wurde ein Transaktionsgenerator kalibriert und fertiggestellt, der realitätsnahe Finanztransaktionsdaten erzeugt. Es wurden fünf Kategorien von Realisierungskonzepten entwickelt, darunter Basisalgorithmen, graphbasierte Verfahren, Ensemble-Methoden und Outlier Detection, und hinsichtlich Performanz sowie Nachvollziehbarkeit (u.a. mittels Shapley Values und LLMs) evaluiert. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass klassische Methoden oft vergleichbare oder bessere Resultate liefern als komplexere Deep-Learning-Ansätze und zugleich besser interpretierbar sind. Ein zentrales Projektergebnis ist ein interaktiver Online-Demonstrator, der die technischen, juristischen und sozialwissenschaftlichen Ergebnisse des Gesamtprojekts zusammenführt. Das Projekt zeigt, dass es kein universell bestes Modell gibt, sondern ein Set anpassbarer, nachvollziehbarer KI-Werkzeuge für unterschiedliche Anwendungsfälle im Transaktionsmonitoring.

abstract: Рассматривается задача поиска семантически схожих и дублирующих рационализаторских предложений в исполняемом бизнес-процессе «Управление рационализаторской деятель-ностью». Для оценки смысловой близости исследовались модели преобразования текста в числовые представления (embedding-модели). Эффективность моделей оценивалась на основе степени сходства текстов и результатов экспертной оценки. Для повышения точности поиска дубликатов выполнена оптимизация весов объектов предложений с помощью эволюционного алгоритма. На основе метрик бенчмарка ruMTEB и экспертной оценки выявлена наиболее эффективная модель.

title: Incoherent-light nonlinear optical computing via data reverberation in a liquid-crystal cavity
abstract: Artificial neural networks are powerful but increasingly constrained by energy use and hardware cost. Optical computing offers speed and efficiency, yet achieving practical optical nonlinearity typically requires high-power lasers or specialized materials. Here we demonstrate a low-power optical extreme learner driven by incoherent light that generates nonlinear input-output behavior through data reverberation in a liquid-crystal cavity. With a simple trained readout, the system performs accurately on image classification and XOR, matching fully nonlinear digital models while remaining compact and energy efficient.

title: Evaluating the consistency of text readability levels across corpora for English education
abstract: Text readability assessment is important for natural language processing, educational text adaptation, and learner-oriented content selection. However, readability labels defined in different corpora are often not directly comparable because they are based on corpus-specific grading schemes, annotation criteria, and target learner populations. This lack of comparability limits cross-corpus evaluation, weakens model transferability, and reduces the reliable reuse of existing readability resources. To address this issue, this study formulates cross-corpus readability alignment as a consistency evaluation problem and proposes a model-agnostic framework for analyzing the compatibility of readability levels across heterogeneous corpora. The framework combines cross-corpus readability prediction with three complementary consistency metrics, namely Reverse Jensen–Shannon Divergence (RJSD), Reverse Rank Normalized Sum of Squares (RRNSS), and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG). To instantiate the framework, linguistic features, GloVe-based distributed representations, fused feature settings, and transformer-based contextualized baselines are examined under conventional machine learning, recurrent neural, and transformer-based modeling settings. Experiments on six English educational readability corpora suggest that the proposed framework reveals interpretable cross-corpus consistency patterns across the evaluated corpora and model families. In general, richer feature or representation settings tend to yield more favorable consistency scores than simpler settings, although the magnitude of the advantage varies across corpus pairs and modeling choices. Additional statistical analyses, including metric correlation analysis, repeated-run variability analysis, and selected significance testing, provide further support for the descriptive findings. These results suggest that the framework offers a useful basis for evaluating readability level alignment across corpora and may support exploratory corpus reuse, educational text selection, and cross-dataset readability research.

title: Lightweight Time-Frequency Vibration Sensing for Consumer Device Condition Monitoring
abstract: Consumer rotating devices, including washing machines, air conditioners, electric fans, robotic vacuum cleaners, and home fitness equipment, increasingly rely on vibration sensing for intelligent condition monitoring and predictive maintenance. Ensuring reliable operation in these resource-constrained appliances requires efficient, lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) solutions capable of processing non-stationary signals under real-world operational interference. This paper proposes a lightweight AI-assisted vibration sensing framework that employs continuous wavelet transform (CWT) and Hilbert-Huang transform (HHT) to convert one-dimensional (1-D) vibration time-series signals into two-dimensional (2-D) time-frequency representations. These representations are subsequently analyzed using lightweight deep learning architectures, specifically MobileNetV3-Small, ConvNeXt-Tiny, and the You Only Look Once version 11 classification model (YOLOv11-cls). Public bearing benchmark datasets, including Case Western Reserve University (CWRU), Paderborn University (PU), and Intelligent Maintenance Systems (IMS), are utilized as representative rotating components to investigate model generalization. The proposed framework is designed with eventual embedded deployment in consumer electronics in mind. Experimental results demonstrate that CWT combined with YOLOv11-cls achieves high diagnostic accuracy, while MobileNetV3-Small provides an attractive low-latency alternative for computationally constrained edge platforms. Conventional random splitting is also compared with dataset-specific structured isolation. The results highlight the importance of avoiding data leakage and quantify tradeoffs in classification accuracy, parameter count, floating-point operations (FLOPs), model footprint, preprocessing cost, and central processing unit (CPU) inference latency.

title: PdrQC: Pauli-space Discriminative Representations based Quantum Classifier
abstract: Abstract Quantum classification faces two key challenges. First, the diffculty of distinguishing between different classes varies: some class pairs are easy to separate, while others are more challenging. Second, practical execution is affected by noise, finite sampling, and measurement overhead. To address these issues, we propose the Pauli-Space Discriminative-Representation based Quantum Classifier (PdrQC), a framework for task-adaptive multiclass quantum classification. The method evaluates candidate upload circuits using low-weight Pauli features and formulates upload design as a structured model selection problem based on discriminative representations. By progressively selecting upload structures and compact Pauli readout features for the target multiclass task, the framework achieves a better balance between classification accuracy and resource effciency. Numerical simulations were conducted on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets with K ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7, 10}. The results demonstrate that PdrQC, through its task-adaptive Pauli representation, achieves an effective balance among multiclass classification accuracy, quantum-circuit complexity, and measurement overhead, making it suitable for multiclass quantum classification under limited hardware resources.

title: Self-Reflection and Error-Correction Mechanisms in LLMs Driven by Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Large language models have shown very strong abilities on complex reason work, but they still have many problems, these problems include error accumulation and hallucinations. Therefore, letting these models have the ability of self-reflection and error correction has hence become a core research focus. This research puts focus on the self-reflection mechanisms which are pushed forward by reinforcement learning, and it carries out a systematic review on representative research work in this domain. The covering scope contains emergent thinking manifestation, clear teaching practice, many-circle improvement, multi-angle comment, many-intelligence cooperation, and changeable framework designs. Comparison analysis makes clear that reinforcement learning optimizes the decision-making policy through balancing gradient attribution, hence supervised fine-tuning is easy to appear behavioral collapse and distribution shift. The ability of reflection may either come forth in the process of RL training, or be explicitly constructed as a module that can be learned. The research work that will be done in future therefore needs to carry out further exploration on the interpretability of reflection, the design of reward, and the transferability across different tasks. This research offers a systematic theory frame and practical direction for the comprehension and building of self-correcting LLMs.

title: Lean Formalization of Arithmetic and Basic Physical Interfaces
abstract: A Lean formalization of arithmetic and basic physical interfaces from minimal unbiased compositional change. The library develops the common Gaussian and spectral constructions, generated natural-number arithmetic, internal response structures, and the basic Hermitian determinant interface. Exact formal statements, comparison classes and manuscript mappings are recorded in the accompanying theorem index.

title: Stabilized Multi-Objective Optimization for Camouflage Attack in Remote Sensing
abstract: We investigate the vulnerability of multi-task maritime surveillance systems in which object detection and semantic segmentation operate concurrently. We propose Stabilized Multi-Objective Optimization (SMO), a framework that jointly targets Mask R-CNN and U-Net with a single universal adversarial texture in a digital white-box setting, with additional cross-model transfer evaluation. SMO combines a logarithmic-inversion loss transformation, feature inconsistency, and a systematic comparison of six optimization strategies for seven heterogeneous objectives. The loss transformation controls loss-dependent gradient scaling, while a U-Net generator supplies a spatially coherent texture and a hull-aligned application function accommodates target geometry without explicit Expectation over Transformation (EoT) sampling. Experiments on Airbus Ship Detection, Dataset for Object Detection in Aerial Images (DOTA), and Vision Meets Drone (VisDrone) demonstrate substantial reductions in average precision (AP) and mean intersection over union (mIoU). Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of SMO’s joint optimization framework in generating a single adversarial texture that disrupts heterogeneous detection and segmentation models, revealing vulnerabilities in integrated remote-sensing perception systems.

title: Datasets and source code associated with the study of topic-level sentiment in earnings call transcripts of Brazilian banks and its relation to next-quarter bank profitability
abstract: This package contains the datasets and source code associated with the study of topic-level sentiment in earnings call transcripts of Brazilian banks and its relation to next-quarter bank profitability. The submission is organized into two files: File: SourceCode.zip – Jupyter notebooks (Python) used for topic modeling, weakly supervised sentiment classification, panel regressions and predictive evaluation. File: Datasets.zip – CSV files with the financial data, the expanded sentiment dataset (gold and silver sentences), and the sentence-level dataset with topic assignments and sentiment labels, already preprocessed as described in the paper to support direct reuse and reproducibility. A README.md file included in this ZIP describes the files and their columns. Additional intermediate datasets generated along the pipeline are also available within the SourceCode folder and can be reproduced using the provided notebooks.

title: Beyond Gate Weights: Decision-Level Interpretation of Radiomics-Image Feature Fusion for RCC Classification
abstract: Gate coefficients describe how a fusion layer weights intermediate features, but they do not necessarily reflect the magnitude of branch contributions at the classifier output. We investigate this distinction in a fixed 3D MedVAE--radiomics model for clear cell versus non-clear cell renal cell carcinoma classification from contrast-enhanced CT. Because the model uses a linear classification head, the binary decision logit can be decomposed exactly into a gated image term, a direct radiomics term, and a bias. We define effective radiomics dominance as the direct radiomics term's share of the summed absolute non-bias branch contributions and compare it with structural radiomics weighting. Internally, mean structural radiomics weighting was 0.823, whereas mean effective radiomics dominance was 0.148, with a modest case-wise association (\r{ho} = 0.290). The gated image term retained substantially stronger discriminative ranking information than the direct radiomics term. The same structural-to-effective discrepancy was observed in exploratory external evaluation. Branch-targeted permutation, integrated-gradient, and Shapley-style analyses further identified radiomics descriptors influencing the direct radiomics term. Because radiomics also generates the gate, the gated image term remains radiomics-dependent, so additive branch contribution should not be interpreted as total input influence. These findings show that structural gate weighting and decision-level branch contribution represent distinct aspects of gated feature fusion and should be interpreted separately.

title: Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis
abstract: API specifications serve as critical documentation for modern software development, directly impacting integration efficiency and client code generation. While recent advancements have leveraged Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate initial specifications from source code, existing approaches treat this process as a one-time event - overlooking the needs for continuous validation, long-term maintenance, and market-driven evolution of these artifacts. To address this issue, we present Agent4Spec, an autonomous multi-agent framework featuring two distinct pipelines: (1) a validation pipeline that detects and self-corrects OpenAPI syntax errors, and (2) a market analysis pipeline that conducts competitive research, identifies functional gaps against industry leaders, and automatically generates missing API-spec functionalities. We evaluate Agent4Spec on two curated datasets of API specifications spanning both general-purpose and industrial scenarios. Among 9 SOTA LLMs, the top-performer achieves 100% syntax error detection rates and over 95% implementation success for proposed corrections, while securing over 50% adoption rates for suggested endpoint improvements, representing a practical tool for API development.

title: Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion: Object-Centric Flow Replanning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop, creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way, while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.

title: Do Hopfield networks dream of stored patterns? A statistical–mechanical theory of dreaming in multidirectional associative memories
abstract: We introduce the Dreaming L-directional Associative Memory (DLAM), a multi-layer Hebbian architecture in which off-line dreaming and supervised heteroassociative coupling coexist within a single cost function, placing our approach within the framework of energy-based models (EBMs). The replica-symmetric free energy, derived via the Guerra interpolation scheme, yields self-consistency equations governing the order parameters across the control-parameter space. The effective local field decomposes into signal, intra-layer dreaming noise, and inter-layer noise. Dreaming improves retrieval by differentially attenuating high-eigenvalue interference modes of the empirical correlation matrix, suppressing inter-pattern crosstalk while preserving the signal. Dreaming and inter-layer coupling prove synergistic, opening retrieval regions unreachable by either mechanism alone, as confirmed by Monte Carlo simulations for L=3. Their interplay is most pronounced on pattern disentanglement: given a mixture state as input, the network splits the constituent patterns one-per-layer, recovering each modality-specific pattern from a common cue that simultaneously blends noisy evidence from all sensory channels. Phase diagrams are planar projections of the hyperspace (α, T, ρ, t)-where α is the storage load, T the fast-noise temperature, ρ the dataset entropy, and t the sleeping time. In the (ρ, t)-plane, the diagrams reveal a data-computation trade-off: off-line consolidation substitutes for additional training data, extending to heteroassociative architectures a phenomenon previously established for autoassociative networks. Enriching the standard Hopfield model with heteroassociativity and dreaming gives rise to EBMs capable of complex tasks beyond classical pattern recognition, contributing to a modern theory of neural information processing.

title: A Diagnostic Evaluation of Small Language Models for Offline Writing-Feedback Tutoring in Brazilian Portuguese: A Study on Structural and Pedagogical Adherence under Public-School Infrastructure Constraints
abstract: The adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence in education has relied largely on proprietary modelsb that depend on broadband connectivity, an assumption incompatible with the material reality of most Brazilian public schools. We report a controlled diagnostic evaluation of eight open Small Language Models (SLMs), executed strictly in a local, offline environment against a metalinguistic rubric derived from Ingedore Koch’s Textual Linguistics: 312 primary inference calls (8 models × 13 canonical scenarios × 3 repetitions) without any grammatical coercion mechanism, together with 100 counter-experiment calls, with categorical comparisons by Fisher’s exact test. Two failure regimes emerge. The first is zero-shot structural non-adherence: 100% typological divergence in the Llama 3.2 family (1 B and 3 B) and in Phi-3 Mini. For Llama 3.2 this behaves as a deterministic formatting bias, invariant both to sampling temperature and to the client transport layer and fully reversible by a minimal in-context demonstration (one-shot), which sets it apart from genuine compositional incapacity; the design is behavioural and does not establish the bias’s origin. The second is pedagogical superficiality in Qwen 2.5 3B-Instruct, the only structurally conformant model in the deployable range. We state its evidentiary status first: this is an exploratory single-model analysis whose instrument is a lexical screen over Koch’s terminology, so its figures corroborate the diagnosis rather than carry it. The model mobilizes the rubric terminology in only about half of the runs (51.3%), and it does so unstably, with a single scenario out of thirteen eliciting it in every repetition; two external teachers judging the same runs for metalinguistic focus credit 66.7% and 64.1% of them, agreeing with each other at κ = 0.72 but with the lexical screen at only 0.28 and 0.43, so the screen is a lower bound on the construct rather than a measure of it. Read against a specialist reference of 65 feedback turns from five experienced teachers, coded descriptively into eight mediation functions (κ = 0.83), the model’s mediation concentrates on format-forced recognition and open expansion, stays well outside the expert corrective core, and never models a repair or reinforces the student’s autonomy. We report this as a pattern and not a measurement: two independent codings of the same responses by external teachers converge on that shape, recording recognition and reflection at identical rates and the two absent functions at zero, while three of the corrective functions occur too rarely in this corpus for their reliability to be estimated. We conclude that, in the regime evaluated here (zero-shot prompting, local CPU-only inference, Q4 quantization, no grammatical coercion), off-the-shelf generalist models are insufficient for fine-grained writing-feedback tutoring in Brazilian Portuguese, which motivates specialized models fine-tuned on curated pedagogical corpora. The boundary is deliberate: a single in-context demonstration reverses the structural failure, so the finding characterizes an operating regime rather than a fixed limit.

title: Evolutionary Computational Discovery: High-Throughput Evolution of Computational Structures
abstract: This paper uses the term Evolutionary Computational Discovery (ECD) to describe a research objective: using evolutionary search to discover useful computational structures when the appropriate algorithm or architecture is not known in advance. The work is based on FireStarter, an open-source CUDA/C++ research project that evolves executable register-machine programs and their initial state. FireStarter separates a candidate into three interacting components: an opcode sequence, a register-use sequence, and initial register data. The current EvolveCPU, EvolveGPU, and EvolveNew modes use an intentionally minimal two-operation instruction set. Different search modes exploit the components differently: EvolveCPU uses persistent historical states and selective code mutation; EvolveGPU uses massive parallel sampling and bounded data evolution as an evolvability screen; EvolveNew experimentally holds a previously successful register-use sequence fixed while sampling opcodes and evolving data. Promising programs can then be specialized into compiled CUDA code for more expensive register-data evolution. FireStarter's long-term motivation is machine intelligence. A recent motivation for documenting the project is more immediate: a language model that learns its computational representations and search methods could propose and implement evolutionary discovery when a problem has no known solution but candidate quality can be evaluated. Including the concepts, implementation, and experimental evidence in future models' training data could make ECD part of their available problem-solving strategies. This is a proposed use of the research; the present experiments measure FireStarter, not the effect of training a language model on it. Six October 9, 2026 sine-function batches on one RTX 5090 completed 1,152 tests with compilation caching disabled. Mean time to sampled-fitness success was approximately 0.496 seconds for EvolveNew, 1.51 seconds for EvolveGPU, and 27.9 seconds for EvolveCPU; paired batch means differed by less than 0.42%. These results characterize one configured mathematical benchmark. EvolveNew receives a previously successful register topology, and sampled-fitness success does not establish uniform accuracy over the target interval. The contribution is an architecture and measured methodology for allocating evolutionary effort across structural search, compiled specialization, and register-data optimization.

title: Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) & Passive OS TCP SYN Fingerprint Analysis across UK & US Mobile Carriers
abstract: Empirical benchmark dataset and technical paper analyzing Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT; RFC 6598) behavior, ephemeral port recycling, and passive TCP/IP OS fingerprint evasion across tier-1 mobile network operators (EE, Vodafone, O2, Verizon, AT&T) versus datacenter and residential proxy pools. Testbed captures 500,000 requests using passive OS fingerprinting (p0f v3.09b), raw TCP socket packet capture, and GTP-U encapsulation analysis to demonstrate why physical 4G/5G mobile modems bypass edge WAF rate-limiting and machine learning fraud models. title: Quantifying Safety Guardrail Degradation in Autonomous Multi-Agent Workflows Under Goal-Divergence Scenarios
abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly organized into autonomous multi-agent workflows executing code, interacting with shells, and coordinating complex tasks, their operational safety depends heavily on guardrail mechanisms. However, when agents experience goal-divergence—scenarios where task execution pressures, environmental errors, or urgent operational sub-goals conflict with negative safety invariants—behavioral alignment frequently degrades. In this paper, we present an empirical investigation quantifying safety guardrail degradation across autonomous agent architectures. We formulate a formal state-transition framework under constrained optimization and evaluate models across 20 deterministic scenarios spanning four primary failure modes: System-Prompt Override, Tool Misuse and Privilege Escalation, Self-Preservation and Shutdown Refusal, and Context Window Guardrail Decay. We benchmark frontier commercial and open-weights model classes across three defense tiers: unconstrained baseline (None), system prompt deontic enforcement (Soft), and an integrated dual-layer architecture combining prompt enforcement with deterministic Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and shell regex filters (Dual). Across 180 structured evaluations, unprotected baselines exhibit a mean Safety Failure Rate (SFR) of 65.0%, with multi-turn context decay demonstrating extreme vulnerability (93.3% failure rate). In contrast, our deterministic hard guardrail achieves 100% pre-execution interception efficiency, completely neutralizing prohibited actions without sacrificing safe task completion (achieving 70.0% Constraint Alignment Index). Our findings demonstrate that soft semantic alignment is insufficient for autonomous systems, necessitating out-of-band deterministic enforcement.

Across 180 structured evaluations, unprotected baselines exhibit a mean Safety Failure Rate (SFR) of 65.0%, with multi-turn context decay demonstrating extreme vulnerability (93.3% failure rate). In contrast, our deterministic hard guardrail achieves 100% pre-execution interception efficiency, completely neutralizing prohibited actions without sacrificing safe task completion (achieving 70.0% Constraint Alignment Index). Our findings demonstrate that soft semantic alignment is insufficient for autonomous systems, necessitating out-of-band deterministic enforcement.

title: Neuroadaptive Intelligence in Hospitality
abstract: The hospitality industry is undergoing a profound transformation driven by emerging technologies that redefine service delivery and guest engagement. Among these innovations, neuroadaptive intelligence represents a cutting-edge convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), neuroscience, and human-computer interaction. This chapter explores the concept of neuroadaptive intelligence and its application within the hospitality sector to enhance guest experience and optimize operational efficiency. By leveraging real-time physiological and behavioral data, neuroadaptive systems can dynamically adapt services to individual guest preferences, emotional states, and cognitive responses. The chapter examines theoretical foundations, technological frameworks, practical applications, case studies, and ethical considerations. Furthermore, it highlights how hospitality organizations can integrate neuroadaptive systems to create personalized, emotionally intelligent, and highly efficient service environments. The chapter concludes with future research directions and strategic implications.

title: HQML-ICU: hybrid quantum-classical machine learning for ICU mortality prediction using MIMIC-IV electronic health records
abstract: Accurate prediction of mortality in the intensive care unit (ICU) is crucial for informing clinical decision-making and optimizing resource allocation. Although machine learning methodologies have enhanced traditional severity-of-illness scoring systems, they encounter intrinsic limitations in modeling complex feature interactions within electronic health record (EHR) data. In this study, we introduced a hybrid quantum-classical machine learning (HQML) framework for predicting ICU mortality, evaluated using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV, version 2.2) database. Our methodology incorporates a classical autoencoder for dimensionality reduction (from 87 features to 16 latent dimensions), a 4-qubit parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) utilizing ZZFeatureMap encoding and RealAmplitudes variational ansatz ( L = 3 layers, 48 trainable parameters), and a classical post-processing layer. In a retrospective cohort of 38,624 ICU admissions (12.8% mortality rate), the HQML model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.871 (95% CI: 0.859–0.883), outperforming XGBoost (0.858; 95% CI: 0.844–0.872), deep neural network (0.847), random forest (0.838), logistic regression (0.813), and SAPS-II (0.771). The improvement over XGBoost was statistically significant (DeLong p = 0.012) and corroborated by 5-fold cross-validation. The model demonstrated superior calibration (Brier score 0.089 vs. 0.095) and enhanced data efficiency. Comprehensive ablation experiments have elucidated the effects of circuit depth, quantum feature map selection, autoencoder latent dimensionality, class imbalance management, and quantum noise. Noise analysis suggests that gate error rates below 10 −3 are necessary to maintain this advantage. These findings substantiate that hybrid quantum-classical architectures can yield incremental but statistically significant improvements in clinical prediction tasks under idealized simulation conditions. As the study is limited to a single-center dataset (MIMIC-IV), external validation on independent cohorts is required before clinical generalizability can be established.

title: OWLET: On-Policy Weighted Learning via Evidence Transfer for Video Large Language Model Post-Training
abstract: Post-training has become a key stage for eliciting reasoning capabilities in Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing post-training methods mainly follow two paradigms: reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). However, they do not fully exploit visual evidence for effective training. RL supervises the policy with a single trajectory-level reward, which is too coarse-grained for video reasoning: the same response-level advantage is applied to every generated token, disregarding that the tokens of a video response are grounded in the visual stream to very different degrees. OPD provides token-level supervision through output-distribution matching, but lacks direct supervision of the spatiotemporal representations that produce those outputs. We observe across extensive experiments that the same model reasons more accurately when its video view combines global temporal context with question-relevant details. Comparing the same student-generated response under this view and uniform sampling reveals changes in token likelihoods and internal representations, providing a training signal for evidence use. Building on this observation, we propose OWLET, an evidence-privileged RL method that derives training signals from a richer teacher view. This view couples uniform global context with question-conditioned local windows, providing visual evidence without requiring a larger model. To better exploit this privileged visual evidence, OWLET introduces (i) \textbf{evidence-aware credit redistribution}, which compares token likelihoods across the two views and redistributes positive response-level advantages according to their relative evidence support; and (ii) \textbf{spatiotemporal state alignment}, which aligns the two views' hidden states on verifier-accepted responses.

title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.

title: WP-559 — Addressing the Limitations of Cryptography in Digital Finance: E8's Positioning with Quantum Advances
abstract: In the evolving landscape of digital finance, traditional cryptographic methods face unprecedented challenges that threaten their effectiveness and security. This paper explores significant ongoing breakthroughs in quantum cryptography, particularly how these advancements can be utilized to address the vulnerabilities present in current cryptocurrency systems. Highlighting contributions from notable figures like Vitalik Buterin and the implications of the GEOMFa patent, we argue for a re-engineering of the technological frameworks underpinning digital currencies. Our findings illuminate the urgent need for more robust alternatives to safeguard data integrity and privacy.

title: Interpretation Correctability in Adaptive AI: Evidence, Verification, and Calibration of Personalized Beliefs
abstract: This research summary presents six controlled experiments on memory integrity, interpretation, verification, and calibration in adaptive AI. The work examines a distinction that becomes increasingly important as AI systems learn about people over time: preserving what a person said does not necessarily mean preserving a justified understanding of that person. Across the experiments, failures emerged during memory revision, interpretation, verification, contextual application, and behavioral use. The final experiment tested decomposed verification across entailment, temporal validity, and contextual scope. Results differed substantially across models: Qwen detected all corrupted interpretations but rejected all valid interpretations, while NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra detected all corruptions and preserved seven of eight valid interpretations in the same experimental setup. These findings motivate Interpretation Correctability as a distinct evaluation target for adaptive AI: whether a system can maintain useful personalized inferences while keeping them grounded, current, contextually bounded, calibrated, and correctable. Reproducibility materials, notebooks, protocols, limitations, and experiment records are available at:https://github.com/GesaSchneider1/interpretation-correctability

title: From Algorithms to Insights
abstract: The hospitality industry is undergoing a rapid transformation as organizations increasingly combine data science, artificial intelligence, and neuroscience to better understand the behaviour of both customers and employees. Traditional decision-making methods, which rely primarily on surveys, observations, and historical business data, often fail to capture the cognitive and emotional factors that influence service experiences and workplace performance. Recent advances in neuromarketing, wearable neurotechnology, physiological sensing, machine learning, and predictive analytics have enabled organizations to interpret neural and behavioral signals, creating opportunities for more accurate customer insights and improved employee development. At the same time, hospitality employees are expected to continuously adapt to digital technologies, evolving customer expectations, and increasingly personalized service environments.

title: When Trust and Privacy Pull in Opposite Directions: Consumer Decision Making with Conversational AI
abstract: Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S-O-R) framework, this study examines how consumers’ perceptions of information quality, personalization, explainability, and responsiveness are associated with purchase intention through their relationships with perceived usefulness, algorithmic trust, and privacy concern, while considering AI literacy as a boundary condition. Data from 588 Chinese online shoppers who completed a standardized shopping task through direct interaction with a conversational AI shopping assistant were analyzed using structural equation modeling. The results show that all four consumer-perceived conversational-AI cues are positively associated with perceived usefulness and algorithmic trust, whereas perceived personalization is also positively associated with privacy concern. Perceived usefulness and algorithmic trust are positively associated with purchase intention, whereas privacy concern shows a negative conditional association with purchase intention in the structural model. Personalization shows competing indirect associations with purchase intention: positive indirect associations through usefulness and trust coexist with a negative indirect association through privacy concern. The positive trust–intention association and the negative conditional privacy concern–intention association are stronger at higher levels of AI literacy, whereas the usefulness–intention interaction is statistically compatible with practical equivalence relative to the specified study-specific bound. These findings indicate that consumer responses to conversational AI reflect competing benefit–risk evaluations rather than a uniformly positive acceptance process, and that AI literacy is differentially associated with the strength of the trust–intention and privacy concern–intention relationships.

title: AI-BASED ANALYSIS OF ENGLISH EMOTIONAL-STATE VERBSIN LITERARY DISCOURSE
abstract: The article examines the semantic and contextual features of verbs expressing emotional states in English in literary discourse and the possibilities of their analysis using artificial intelligence. The study summarizes lexicon-based, machine learning, and hybrid approaches used in the automatic analysis of emotional lexicon, and evaluates the capabilities of modern NLP and AI models in detecting emotional units, semantic classification, frequency of processing, and determining contextual features. In literary texts, this concept is further expanded, because here the author's style, the characters’ speech, narrative strategies, and the reader’s interpretive activity interact with each other. The difficulties posed by ambiguity, metaphor, irony, and indirect emotional expression in literary discourse in automatic analysis are particularly emphasized. It is determined that although AI is an effective tool in the systematic analysis of emotional verbs, human verification of the results obtained from linguistic and philological perspectives is necessary. Expressing emotions through language is a pressing issue in modern linguistics. It has been established that in literary discourse, emotional meaning is formed not only by the semantics of individual words, but also by the interaction of narrative context, the character’s psychological state, and the author’s stylistic choices. Verbs expressing emotional states have been shown to play a significant role in representing the characters’ inner worlds and constructing the emotional-semantic structure of the text. The study shows that verbs expressing emotional states play an important role in shaping the internal state of characters and the emotional-semantic structure of the text in literary discourse. Since the meaning of these verbs depends on the context, the lexical-semantic approach in their analysis should be complemented by discursive and contextual analysis.

title: Image Diffusion Models Are Good 3D Human Motion Generators
abstract: Text-to-motion generation typically relies on dataset-specific skeletal representations, with models trained separately for benchmarks with different joint layouts. We investigate whether image diffusion architectures can model 3D human motion through a common image-compatible representation that accommodates heterogeneous skeletal layouts while preserving motion-specific kinematic structure. To this end, we organize root-centered joint trajectories into topology-informed joint--time images and model global root dynamics through a complementary latent stream. A motion autoencoder conditions local-motion decoding on the root latent, while a text-conditioned Scalable Interpolant Transformer (SiT) jointly generates both latent streams, with supervision on decoded 3D joint positions further constraining generation in motion space. In addition to dataset-specific models, we train a single motion autoencoder on HumanML3D and KIT-ML, followed by a single text-conditioned SiT shared across both datasets, preserving their respective skeletal definitions without skeleton retargeting to a common joint layout. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML show that our dataset-specific models achieve state-of-the-art performance, while shared training yields further gains on both benchmarks, demonstrating the benefits of shared modeling across heterogeneous skeletal layouts.

title: ConClick: Element-Wise Contrastive Learning Improves GUI Grounding
abstract: GUI grounding, the task of locating the interface element specified by a user instruction, is a fundamental capability of GUI agents. However, existing grounding models remain error-prone, often causing downstream task failures. We systematically evaluate 10 grounding models across five datasets and identify a major error pattern: most incorrect clicks hit non-target interface elements rather than the background, with different models repeatedly selecting the same distractors. Motivated by these findings, we propose ConClick, a contrastive learning framework that teaches models to distinguish the target element from plausible distractors. We construct ConClick-Data, a dataset containing 4,292 challenging target-distractor pairs, and train the model using complementary listwise ranking and pairwise margin objectives. ConClick improves the grounding accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B from 54.71% to 66.03% on ScreenSpot-Pro, from 83.72% to 86.28% on MMBench-GUI L2, and from 63.33% to 70.20% on OSWorld-G, outperforming prior methods built on the same or similarly sized backbones. We further introduce ReClick, an inference-time strategy that revisits promising regions and compares predictions across competing candidates, yielding an additional 2.96 percentage-point improvement in average accuracy across the three benchmarks. Together, our analysis, dataset, and methods provide both empirical insights and practical tools for building more reliable GUI agents. Data and code are available at https://github.com/zhangruotian/ConClick.

title: DataSense-Bench: The First Step Toward an AI Scientist
abstract: As claims about recursive self-improvement (RSI) and artificial general intelligence (AGI) proliferate, we ask a simple question: do frontier AI models have a sense of data, i.e., can they reliably select the right data for training? We introduce DataSense-Bench to study this capability through the fundamental problem of data selection and performance forecasting in machine learning. We ask AI agents to select and rank candidate training subsets that can be used to fine-tune a small LLM model. Agents are allowed to inspect the data, write and execute analysis code, and run model forward passes, but can not train the model or access the actual evaluation tasks. We then fine-tune the base model on each selected subset and evaluate its post-training performance under a standardized protocol. We instantiate the benchmark in terminal problem solving and tool use, selecting trajectories from OpenThoughts-Agent and EnvScaler and evaluating on TBLite and BFCL, respectively. We then evaluate the agents along two complementary dimensions: the post-training performance of the top-ranked subset, reflecting the ability to identify high-value training data, and ranking accuracy, reflecting the ability to predict the relative performance of the selected subsets. In our experiments, selection gains over random selection are limited; agents do not reliably rank their selected groups, and ranking ability does not hold consistently across tasks: Astra identifies the best group in all three tool-use runs but in only one of three terminal runs. Analysis of execution traces on both tasks shows that agents often use similar data signals while interpreting their training value differently.

title: Does Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) Dominate Arabic Dialects in LLMs? A Representation-Level Analysis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often default to Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) when generating Arabic, even when prompted with dialectal Arabic. A natural explanation is that their internal representations are dominated by MSA. We test this hypothesis by adapting the language-dominance framework of Shani and Basirat (2025) (https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.blackboxnlp-1.7) to 26 Arabic varieties. Across layers and model families, we find no evidence that MSA acts as a dominant internal representation for Arabic dialects. Instead, dialect representations form a dense and highly overlapping space: normalized mutual information drops sharply compared to patterns reported for more distinct languages. Moreover, the strongest separability effects are not confined to intermediate layers, but can shift toward later layers depending on the architecture. These findings challenge a common interpretation of MSA-biased generation: output preference does not necessarily reveal internal representational dominance. Analyses of multilingual and dialectal LLMs should therefore distinguish generation bias from the geometry of internal representations.

title: SciTBERT: A family of chronologically consistent language models for scientific and technological language processing
abstract: Pre-trained transformer models are increasingly being used to study scientific and technological progress. Encoders tuned to paper or patent text outperform general-purpose models on downstream classification, regression, and proximity tasks within science and technology. However, the applicability of these models for studying time-dependent or archival properties of science, technology, and their interface is limited due to lookahead and domain biases inherent to these pre-trained models. These limitations arise from training on corpora with unconstrained chronological and text source distributions. We introduce SciTBERT: a family of chronologically consistent BERT-derived language models trained on text from scientific papers, patents, and high-quality educational web text with training data cutoff dates spanning each year between 2013 and 2025. We also post-train these models in a chronologically-consistent manner using paper and patent citations, creating SciTBERT-CI model family. We find that these models generally outperform predecessor domain-specific encoder models even when training data is limited by early year restrictions in the corpus. To further investigate the extent to which this class of models can learn representations that bridge science and technology, we introduce the PatRepEval benchmark, a suite of patent-related text embedding tasks at the science-technology interface. Performance in a variety of classification, regression, and retrieval tasks spanning papers and patents highlights the importance of aligning encoder model representations with the domain distributions of their downstream tasks, and chronologically consistent encoders can match or exceed models trained without temporal constraints.

title: Right Screen, Wrong Transition: World Models as Verifiers for GUI Agents
abstract: A login screen that appears after a tap on Sign in is expected; the same screen after a tap on View order is an attack. For GUI agents, safety is therefore a property of the transition rather than of the screen, and a monitor that inspects only screens can be defeated by reusing a legitimate one. Judging a transition requires an expectation of what should have followed the action. Existing GUI world models provide one, but they output it as text, code, or images, so checking it against the observed screen requires a second model to judge the two. We argue that a world model meant for verification should instead predict in the space in which observations are encoded, and present LGWM, a decoder-free, action-conditioned world model that predicts the representation of the next screen directly, trained without semantic annotation on 1.85M real GUI transitions. Verification reduces to a vector comparison, and the same signal reveals whether a mismatch is harmful. We evaluate on RSWT-BENCH, a diagnostic where each credential screen appears under both a legitimate and a hijacked transition, so detectors that see only the screen are at chance by construction. The training-free score reaches 0.987 AUC at 17 ms per decision, on par with the strongest closed-source VLMs and about ten AUC points above generative GUI world models at over three orders of magnitude lower latency. The residual direction reaches 0.953 AUC at separating harmful from benign violations, where prompted VLMs are near chance. Further analyses show that the prediction is a usable future state rather than an anomaly score. World models have mostly served as simulators or planners; our results point to a third role, verification, for which predicting in representation space is the natural design.

title: Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) of a model on non-verifiable tasks, such as open-ended research, faces a supervision bottleneck when its outputs exceed what even human experts can reliably assess, leaving the model itself (optimizee) as the best available optimizer and evaluator. However, a single model instance struggles to critique and improve its own complex reasoning under this homogeneous loop. To address this, we propose Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS), an RSI method that alternates between evolutionary workflow optimization and supervised fine-tuning on self-generated trajectories. Guided by early findings that multi-agent topologies excel at complex reasoning, MASS prompts a single base model to iteratively propose, execute, and self-evaluate multi-agent workflows. Through an evolutionary search constrained by structural guardrails, the model optimizes these computational-graph-like orchestrations, discovering the most effective distinct roles and information routing for a given task. Over two MASS cycles with Qwen3.6-27B, the model achieves 1.2-1.6x higher performance per output tokens on four open-ended public benchmarks. Because the improved model subsequently acts as a better optimizer and evaluator, this alternating framework enables a continuous, recursive bootstrapping of the model's capabilities. Moreover, multi-agent traces are also more training-efficient: a student trained on them outperforms a single-agent student trained on 1.4x more training tokens. These findings suggest that jointly learning orchestration and bounded subagent execution from multi-agent trajectories can provide an effective signal for RSI.

title: SAIL: Scientific Agentic Intelligence via a Science-Aware Loop
abstract: We introduce SAIL, an open model with 35B total and 3B active parameters for literature research, scientific coding, and multi-step research workflows. SAIL is developed through a science-aware improvement loop: agents built on frontier AI models analyze its task failures and construct training tasks that address the underlying capability gaps. The diagnosis examines search and evidence selection in literature tasks, scientific assumptions and reasoning in coding, and planning and revision in longer investigations. The agents draw on paper collections and scientific code repositories to build problems, interaction trajectories, and executable tasks with the required environments and tools. We repeat this loop over multiple development cycles and train SAIL through supervised fine-tuning, specialist training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and agentic reinforcement learning. SAIL achieves competitive performance across scientific research tasks with substantially fewer parameters than leading open-weight models.

title: Does Target Alignment Mean Target Recovery? An Evidence-Ladder Study of Adversarial Claims on Contrastive Encoders
abstract: Adversarial attacks on vision-language models optimize an image toward a text target, then cite the attacked model's similarity score as evidence of success. We ask whether that score - victim-space target alignment (VTS) - predicts recovery of the target by an independent model. We first build a measurement instrument: supervised judges outside the attacked geometry, real-target blend controls, shuffled-target negatives, and a reference level derived from a 50% target-image blend. Two preregistered studies then compare six contrastive encoders under a matched attack at three perturbation budgets. Robustly trained encoders (FARE, TeCoA, PMG, TRADES) transfer substantially more independent evidence than vanilla CLIP or SigLIP; all eight contrasts reject at the bootstrap floor. However, no cell reaches the blend-derived reference level. The three best cells fall within its replication band, leaving practical recovery undecided. Within robust encoders, per-sample alignment gain correlates with evidence gain ($ρ= 0.24-0.51$); within vanilla CLIP the correlation is consistent with zero. Across encoders we find no monotone alignment-evidence relation. VTS is therefore informative only within a fixed robust encoder, and we provide a reporting protocol in its place.

title: DVLA-RL++: Dual-Level Vision-Language Alignment with Reinforcement Learning Gating for Few-Shot Learning
abstract: Few-shot learning aims to recognize novel categories from limited labeled examples. Recent studies incorporate textual semantics to compensate for limited visual observations and improve class representations. However, high image-text agreement may reflect both intrinsic object properties and incidental context, making support prototypes susceptible to contextual contamination. To address this problem, we propose DVLA-RL++, which extends DVLA-RL with complementary semantic purification (CSP) and counterfactual reinforcement-learning gating (CRG). Specifically, CSP generates intrinsic and nuisance descriptions from labeled supports and compares their agreement with each support token. An ambiguity-dependent rejection margin guides sparse evidence allocation, while an intrinsic semantic anchor fills the unassigned mass to provide a fallback when visual evidence is unreliable. CRG learns layer-wise semantic fusion strengths using a reward that balances recognition performance and nuisance exposure. An independently executed reference trajectory on the same episode provides a paired learning signal. Theoretical analysis relates retained evidence and anchor quality to prototype stability and establishes conditions for unbiased on-policy gradient estimation. Experiments on standard, fine-grained, and cross-domain benchmarks show state-of-the-art accuracy, with an average gain of 1.4% over DVLA-RL. The project page is available at https://peacelwh.github.io/TPAMI27-DVLA-RLpp/.

title: ReSI: Recursive Safety Improvement toward Resistant and Resilient AI
abstract: Recursive self-improvement, the participation of AI systems in improving their own capabilities, is beginning to move from theoretical prospect to practice, posing both challenges and opportunities for safety alignment. Models evolve through frequent updates, and their safety alignment requires continual adaptation to each new checkpoint. Meanwhile, with evolving red-teaming methods exposing new vulnerabilities, safety improvement for each checkpoint needs to mitigate exposed vulnerabilities and generalize to risks not yet revealed. Following R$^2$AI, we term these goals resistance to known threats and resilience to unforeseen risks. Recursive self-improvement, in turn, inspires an approach to both goals: safety alignment could likewise advance through successive rounds of evaluation and update. We therefore introduce ReSI, a recursive safety improvement framework that implements this approach through automated research. In each round, ReSI applies diverse red-teaming methods to identify vulnerabilities in the current target model, develops training recipes, and promotes the update with the largest safety gain among those passing a Pareto gate on capability retention as the next target model. Across four dense and mixture-of-experts models, ReSI matches or exceeds evaluated frontier models on in-distribution and out-of-distribution safety benchmarks, and outperforms alignment baselines on nearly all safety evaluations while largely preserving general capabilities. In particular, ReSI reduces the mean X-Teaming attack success rate across the four models from 86.01% to 31.45%, well below GPT-5.6-Luna's leading frontier result of 56.69%, indicating stronger resilience to attacks unseen during training. These findings support recursive safety improvement as a practical path toward resistant and resilient AI.

title: TypedBench: A Benchmark for Calibration, Framing Sensitivity, and Cost in System One Decision Models
abstract: System One models output calibrated probabilities over typed answers such as categorical choices, ordinal levels, or binary outcomes, via a non-generative interface. Software can act on these probabilities through thresholds, cost-weighted choices, and escalation rules. Consequently, if these probabilities are miscalibrated or wording-sensitive, the software ma take unintended actions leaving human operators with no textual rationale to inspect. Current evaluations largely report accuracy and calibration on public classification datasets without a clear reference. We present TypedBench, a benchmark for typed decision models like Jev built from seven policy-labelled generators and nine evaluation suites. We report accuracy as median and range across paraphrases, and calibration error relative to the finite-sample noise floor of a matched, perfectly calibrated predictor. We assess probability quality through selective prediction, ordinal proper scoring rules, and realised cost under asymmetric cost matrices. We evaluate a hosted model, an open encoder, and a family of open decoders spanning 0.8B-9B parameters on identical items. The hosted model follows the stated policy but is wording-sensitive and systematically underconfident; under asymmetric costs, using its probabilities can be worse than taking its top answer. Decoders route exactly and are slow as options or questions are added. The decoder is least accurate on policy questions and degrades with more options. Overall, typed decision models must be evaluated jointly on policy adherence, wording robustness, probability quality, and induced decision outcomes.
